claims.text: Controlled heat treatment or thermomechanical processing can enhance short-range chemical ordering in corrosion-resistant steels.
Heat-treatment-induced short-range ordering causes chromium to segregate preferentially to surfaces, grain boundaries, and defects.
Chromium segregation promotes formation of a stable, chromium-rich passive oxide film.
The chromium-rich passive film is continuous and adherent.
The chromium-rich passive film can consist of Cr2O3.
A dense chromium-rich oxide film acts as a diffusion barrier that limits ingress of aggressive species.
Limiting ingress of aggressive species reduces electrochemical dissolution and the effective corrosion rate.
As-cast or as-rolled low-alloy and stainless steels have a uniform, random solid-solution distribution of alloying elements.
The steels under consideration contain approximately 10–20% chromium.
A temperature of about 320°C and pressure of 11.3 MPa are representative test conditions for a PWR primary-water environment.
Heat-treated specimens will have lower corrosion current densities than untreated specimens under identical exposure conditions.
Heat-treated specimens will exhibit less corrosion-associated weight loss than untreated specimens.
Heat-treated specimens will develop a more homogeneous chromium-rich passive film than untreated specimens.
Heat-treated specimens will develop a thicker chromium-rich passive film than untreated specimens.
Untreated steels with randomly distributed chromium form thinner and less uniform oxide films.
The proposed mechanism requires a sufficient chromium concentration, typically greater than 10%.
The proposed mechanism should operate only under conditions where passivation is thermodynamically favorable.
The mechanism may fail in highly aggressive, non-passivating environments where selective alloy-element dissolution dominates corrosion.
